questions.stem: A bag contains 3 red, 4 blue, and 5 yellow balls. One ball is drawn at random. What is the probability that the ball drawn is NOT yellow?

options.option_text: 5/12 — the probability of drawing a yellow ball, not its complement
7/12 — since 7 of the 12 balls in the bag are not yellow
7/11 — dividing non-yellow count by total after removing one yellow
5/7 — ratio of yellow balls to non-yellow balls in the bag

questions.explanation: Total balls = 3+4+5 = 12. Non-yellow balls = 3+4 = 7. P(not yellow) = 7/12. Option A (5/12) is the probability of drawing a yellow ball — a complementary confusion. Option C (7/11) wrongly subtracts one yellow ball from the total before the draw, misapplying conditional-probability logic.

questions.stem: A card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled deck of 52 cards. What is the probability that the card bears an ODD number (Aces are NOT counted as odd)?

options.option_text: 5/13 — if Ace is also treated as an odd-numbered card
3/13 — mistakenly omitting 7 from the list of odd numbers
4/13 — counting 3, 5, 7, 9 across all four suits (16 cards)
2/13 — limiting the count to only red-suited odd-numbered cards

questions.explanation: Odd-numbered cards (Ace excluded): 3, 5, 7, 9 — each in 4 suits = 16 cards. P = 16/52 = 4/13. Option A (5/13) is the classic trap of counting Ace as odd, giving 5×4=20 cards. Option B (3/13) arises when a student forgets to include 7, leaving only three odd values.

questions.stem: A committee of 2 members is to be selected at random from a group of 5 men and 3 women. What is the probability that the committee includes AT LEAST ONE woman?

options.option_text: 9/14 — using complementary method: 1 minus P(no woman selected)
3/8 — direct probability of selecting a woman in a single draw
15/28 — counting only committees with exactly one woman
3/28 — probability of selecting exactly two women on the committee

questions.explanation: Total ways = C(8,2) = 28. All-male committees = C(5,2) = 10. P(at least 1 woman) = 1 − 10/28 = 18/28 = 9/14. Option C (15/28) is the most tempting error — it counts only exact-one-woman cases: C(5,1)×C(3,1) = 15, ignoring the two-women case C(3,2) = 3, thus giving 15/28 instead of 18/28.

questions.stem: Two unbiased dice are thrown simultaneously. What is the probability that the ABSOLUTE DIFFERENCE between the two numbers shown is exactly 2?

options.option_text: 5/18 — probability that the absolute difference equals 1, not 2
1/9 — counting only pairs where the smaller number appears first
1/6 — applying a single-die probability formula to two dice
2/9 — all 8 ordered pairs with absolute difference of exactly 2

questions.explanation: Ordered pairs with |a−b|=2: (1,3),(3,1),(2,4),(4,2),(3,5),(5,3),(4,6),(6,4) — exactly 8 of 36. P = 8/36 = 2/9. Option A (5/18) is the probability for |a−b|=1, which yields 10 ordered pairs — the most frequent error from misidentifying the target difference. Option B (1/9) forgets to count both orderings of each pair.

questions.stem: A box contains 10 bulbs, of which 3 are defective. Two bulbs are drawn one by one WITHOUT replacement. Given that the FIRST bulb drawn is defective, what is the probability that the SECOND bulb is also defective?

options.option_text: 3/10 — using the original proportion without updating the sample
2/9 — 2 defective bulbs remain among 9 after the first is drawn
1/15 — computing the joint probability that both are defective
1/5 — keeping the original total of 10 in the denominator

questions.explanation: After removing the first defective bulb, 9 bulbs remain with exactly 2 still defective. Conditional probability = 2/9. Option A (3/10) is the unconditional probability of picking a defective bulb — it ignores the given condition. Option C (1/15) is the joint probability C(3,2)/C(10,2) = 3/45 = 1/15, which answers a different question.

questions.stem: The probabilities that students A, B, and C each independently pass an examination are 1/2, 1/3, and 1/4 respectively. What is the probability that EXACTLY TWO of the three students pass?

options.option_text: 1/24 — probability that all three students pass simultaneously
7/24 — probability that at least two of the three students pass
1/4 — summing three mutually exclusive two-pass combinations
1/8 — counting only the case where both A and B pass the exam

questions.explanation: Three mutually exclusive cases: P(A∩B∩C') = (1/2)(1/3)(3/4) = 3/24; P(A∩B'∩C) = (1/2)(2/3)(1/4) = 2/24; P(A'∩B∩C) = (1/2)(1/3)(1/4) = 1/24. Total = 6/24 = 1/4. Option B (7/24) is the probability that at least two pass — it adds the all-three-pass case (1/24) to the exact-two total, a classic 'at least' vs 'exactly' confusion.

questions.stem: Box A contains 3 red and 5 white balls; Box B contains 4 red and 2 white balls. A fair coin is tossed: heads → draw from Box A, tails → draw from Box B. A red ball is drawn. What is the probability it came from Box B?

options.option_text: 16/25 — Bayes' theorem applied correctly to the red-ball evidence
9/25 — the posterior probability that the red ball came from Box A
1/2 — the prior probability before observing the ball's colour
2/3 — Box B's own conditional probability without normalising

questions.explanation: P(Red|A)=3/8, P(Red|B)=2/3, each box chosen with P=1/2. Total P(Red) = (3/8)(1/2)+(2/3)(1/2) = 3/16+1/3 = 9/48+16/48 = 25/48. Bayes: P(B|Red) = [(2/3)(1/2)]÷(25/48) = (1/3)×(48/25) = 16/25. Option B (9/25) is P(Box A|Red), the complementary posterior. Option D (2/3) is Box B's likelihood before normalising across both hypotheses.
